source: Alamdari, Cao, Wilson (2024) Jump Starting Bandits with LLM-Generated Prior Knowledge (CBLI)
finding: An LLM is asked to simulate users and their rewards. The bandit is pre-trained on that synthetic data, then learns online. So the LLM acts as a prior, not as the chooser. Early regret falls. Gains shrink as real data arrives.
numbers: Experiment 1 (LLM oracle, charity-message arms): 14 to 17 percent lower cumulative regret at T=1000. Experiment 2 (real conjoint survey, sleeping bandit): 19 to 20 percent; 14.8 percent with privacy-sensitive attributes withheld. Table 1: pre-training on 100, 500, 1000 LLM-made users gives growing but diminishing reductions (cosine-similarity baseline 5.43 +/- 0.26 percent). Table 2: GPT-3.5 13.79 to 19.65 percent, Claude-3 Haiku 14.51 to 20.39 percent across 100, 1000, 10000 synthetic users.
quote: significantly reduces online learning regret and data-gathering costs
limits: Contextual (linear) bandit with user features, not a few-arm operator bandit. T=1000 to 9855, far above our 20 to 60 pulls. Compared only to no pre-training and a similarity baseline, not to a hand-set prior or to the LLM choosing. The authors say the generated data does not perfectly mirror human preferences.
agent_relevance: First direct evidence on gap 9. An LLM-made prior can cut early regret by about 15 to 20 percent versus a cold start at T=1000. Nobody has tested it against LLM-as-chooser or at 30 pulls. Cheap design: ask the model for pseudo-counts per operator, cap their strength, let outcomes override.

source: Kveton, Konobeev, Zaheer, Hsu, Mladenov, Boutilier, Szepesvari (2021) Meta-Thompson Sampling (ICML)
finding: Thompson sampling needs a prior. If the prior is unknown, MetaTS learns it across tasks. The authors also test deliberately wrong meta-priors (too wide by 3x, too narrow by a third).
numbers: m=20 tasks, horizon n=200 rounds per task, 100 runs, K=2 (Bernoulli, Gaussian) and K=5d (linear, d=2,4,8). Misspecified MetaTSx3 and MetaTS/3: misspecification changes regret, sometimes in the good direction, with no catastrophic failure.
quote: we do not observe catastrophic failures
limits: Horizon 200 and K=2 for the two simple problems; synthetic. The misspecification tested is a width change of the meta-prior, not a prior pointing at the wrong arm. The prior-gap term in the bound is O(n^2) in horizon, which the authors call unfortunate.
agent_relevance: Supports learning the operator prior from past tasks instead of guessing it. Says little about a wrong prior that favours the wrong operator at 30 pulls (see d03 and d16).

source: Simchowitz, Tosh, Krishnamurthy, Hsu, Lykouris, Dudik, Schapire (2021) Bayesian decision-making under misspecified priors with applications to meta-learning
finding: Proves how much Thompson sampling loses when its prior is wrong, in terms of total-variation distance between priors and the horizon H. The bound is tight in the worst case.
numbers: Corollary 3.1: |R(TS with true prior) - R(TS with wrong prior)| <= 2 H^2 * TV(P, P') * B for B-bounded priors. The authors note frequentist TS guarantees focus on long horizons and are less relevant for many short-horizon tasks.
limits: Worst case, quadratic in H. It does not say a wrong prior is harmless at 30 pulls; it caps the loss by a quantity that grows fast with H. Simulations in the paper use structured priors, not operator pools.
agent_relevance: Theory for gap 5: the cost of a wrong prior grows with horizon squared, so short runs are the safest place for a modest prior, but the bound is loose. Keep prior strength to a few pseudo-counts and test it empirically.

source: Maturana, Fialho, Saubion, Schoenauer, Sebag (2009) Extreme Compass and Dynamic Multi-Armed Bandits for Adaptive Operator Selection (CEC)
finding: Compares credit rules inside a bandit selector on SAT local search with 6 operators. A racing procedure (F-Race) over 225 settings keeps only configurations whose main window uses the EXTREME reward (max of last 10), not the average. Extreme credit plus bandit beats uniform choice on all 22 instances.
numbers: Racing survivors A to D all use an Extreme window of size 10 for the main measure; the second window type did not matter. 50 runs x 22 SAT instances, Student t at 95 percent. Table III: best combination beats Uniform Choice 22-0 (instances won-lost), Compass 18-2, Ex-DMAB 21-0. Table IV mean false clauses: f1000 ExCoDyMAB 10.3 vs Compass 30.9, Ex-DMAB 16.4, Uniform 55.8; Par16 15.2 vs 64.0, 24.1, 131.1.
quote: emphasizes the need to identify rare-but-good improvements
limits: Thousands of evaluations per run, 6 operators, fitness is a count of unsatisfied clauses. Parameters were tuned by racing on the same instances, so the margin is optimistic. Window size is landscape dependent by the authors' own words. Not a Thompson sampler.
agent_relevance: Best direct support for gap 2: a max over the last 10 gains beats the mean as credit when improvements are rare and large. Our operators also give rare large gains. But see d05: extreme credit makes a bandit favour high-variance operators.

source: Fialho, Da Costa, Schoenauer, Sebag (2010) Analyzing bandit-based adaptive operator selection mechanisms (Ann. Math. Artif. Intell.)
finding: Tests instantaneous, average and extreme credit with four selectors (Adaptive Pursuit, MAB, sliding MAB, dynamic MAB) on artificial two-operator scenarios and Royal Road. Extreme credit makes every bandit rule risk-taking, favouring high-variance operators. Average credit is unbiased.
numbers: Artificial scenario ART(0.1,39,0.5,3), epochs T=50, 200, 500, 2000, 50 runs. Best selector in all four: dynamic MAB with Extreme reward. Table 4a (T=50; naive uniform total 1700, optimal 2400): MAB instantaneous 1869, DMAB 1869, sliding MAB about 1980 to 2040, AP 1724. Table 4b (T=200; naive 6800, optimal 9600): sliding MAB extreme 8746 vs average 8522; DMAB extreme 8834. Text: Extreme performs slightly better than Average and Instantaneous, especially for large T. Gain over naive grows with T.
quote: For all bandit-based Operator Selection rules, the Extreme Credit Assignment mechanism is risk-taker
limits: Each cell tuned per setting (C, window, restart threshold) by racing, so tuned-vs-untuned. At the shortest epoch (T=50) the best bandits close about 30 to 40 percent of the gap between naive and optimal. Ten epochs per run. PDF table layout is garbled, so only clearly readable values are quoted.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 8: at 50 pulls per regime the best rule recovers only part of the headroom, and extreme credit helps mostly when T is large. For a few dozen pulls extreme credit is not shown to beat plain binary improvement, and it risks locking onto a noisy high-variance operator.

source: Fialho, Schoenauer, Sebag (2010) Toward Comparison-based Adaptive Operator Selection (GECCO)
finding: Credits operators by rank (Sum of Ranks) or by Area Under the Curve of the sorted reward list, instead of raw fitness gain. Result: invariant to monotone fitness transformations and much less sensitive to hyper-parameters. Fed into a UCB selector (AUC-B, SR-B) they are only beaten by the highly tuned dynamic MAB.
numbers: Tested on OneMax and artificial Boolean and Outlier scenarios. Conclusion: AUC-B and SR-B are only outperformed by DMAB (highly sensitive to hyper-parameters) and are better than most earlier AOS methods on both scenarios.
limits: OneMax and artificial scenarios only; I did not extract numeric tables. Rank credit loses magnitude information, which Ex-DMAB found useful.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: rank-based credit is the most robust choice when reward scales differ across tasks and states (ours do). It removes the need to tune reward normalisation.

source: Own paired analysis of Ashizawa et al. (2025) OPTS, Table 2 (DE optimiser, Llama-3-8B, 27 BBH tasks)
finding: I redid the Thompson-vs-uniform comparison at task level, using the 27 per-task scores in Table 2 (each a mean of 3 seeds). The gap is positive and passes simple tests across tasks.
numbers: Means 53.87 (uniform) vs 55.67 (TS), difference +1.79 points. Paired over 27 tasks: sd of differences 3.57, t = 2.61 (df 26, p about 0.015); TS higher on 18 tasks, lower on 7, tied on 2; sign test p = 0.043; Wilcoxon signed-rank (normal approximation) z = 2.66, p = 0.008.
limits: Task is the unit; seeds are averaged out, so this tests 'across tasks', not 'across seeds'. Per-task seed sd averages about 3.2 (uniform) and 3.6 (TS) points, so single-task differences are noise. Only 3 seeds underlie each cell. One prompt designer, one dev/test protocol. Both arms use the same iteration budget, so it does not settle 'equal API calls'.
agent_relevance: Closes part of gap 6 for the DE optimiser: Thompson over uniform is probably real on average (about +1.8 points) but small against task-to-task noise. Expect about a third of tasks to go the other way.

source: Own paired analysis of Ashizawa et al. (2025) OPTS, Table 10 (GA optimiser, Llama-3-8B, 27 BBH tasks)
finding: Same test on the GA optimiser. The Thompson advantage disappears.
numbers: Means 52.89 (uniform) vs 53.48 (TS), +0.60. Over 27 tasks: sd of differences 3.25, t = 0.96; TS higher on 12, lower on 14, tied on 1; sign test p = 0.85; Wilcoxon z = 0.57, p = 0.57.
limits: Rows were parsed from a garbled PDF layout; the column means reproduce the printed averages (52.89 and 53.48), which checks the parse. Same limits as d07.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 answer: the Thompson edge depends on the optimiser. With DE it is +1.8 and significant across tasks; with GA it is +0.6 and indistinguishable from zero. Always keep a uniform control.

finding: Ablates three adaptation levels in an LLM-driven evolutionary search. Removing the stall-triggered meta-guidance (a prompt-level directive injected when all islands stagnate) hurts most. Replacing the bandit island selector with round robin hurts less.
numbers: Mean of 3 runs. Circle packing: full 2.6294 (sd 0.003); w/o local adaptation 2.5906; w/o adaptive (bandit) island selection 2.6180; w/o meta-guidance 2.5213; fixed 2 islands 2.6187; fixed 5 islands 2.5891. Signal processing: full 0.7178; w/o local 0.6807; w/o bandit island selection 0.619; w/o meta-guidance 0.5476; fixed 2 islands 0.5512; fixed 5 islands 0.6085.
limits: 3 runs, two tasks, no significance test. The stall trigger injects new instructions; it does not just switch operator. The bandit here chooses islands, not operators. No stall-only variant is run.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a stall-triggered change to what the model is told was worth more than a bandit rule in this system (circle packing drop 0.108 vs 0.011; signal processing 0.170 vs 0.099). It does not isolate a plain forced operator switch at equal tokens.

source: Deliberate Evolution (2026) ablation Table 4 and operator policy (Section 3)
finding: The operator policy is a hand-built, state-keyed multiplicative-weights rule: the parent's state (two binary flags, 4 states) indexes a categorical policy over operators, updated by the relative improvement of the offspring over its parent, with an exploration floor. A separate stagnation monitor shifts to exploratory operators. The ablation says the state-keyed policy matters far more than the stagnation monitor.
numbers: Physics set, Qwen3-4B (NMSE, Acc0.01): full 4.37e-4, 15.91 percent; fixed refine operator 8.69e-3, 9.52; uniform operator sampling 1.02e-2, 6.82; without stagnation monitor 7.69e-4, 13.64; without memory 1.34e-3, 9.52; without tool 2.52e-2, 4.55. Separate 3-run check: mean NMSE 4e-4, variance 9e-10 for Qwen3-4B.
limits: The ablation table does not state its number of runs. Domain is symbolic regression with a 4B model; state flags are hand designed; the full system also has memory and tools. Not a bandit, no regret analysis. The state-keyed rule is not compared with a global (state-free) learned rule.
agent_relevance: Evidence on gaps 2, 3 and 4 together. A state-keyed policy with relative-improvement reward beats uniform by about 23x in NMSE, while removing the stall monitor costs 1.8x. So here a state-conditioned policy outweighs a stall trigger, which cuts against the first reading of gap 3. Still missing: state-keyed vs global bandit.

source: Fiandri, Metelli, Trovo (2025) Sliding-Window Thompson Sampling for Non-Stationary Settings (JAIR)
finding: Regret analysis and tests for Beta-SWTS and a Gaussian version with window tau. Theory sets the window near sqrt(T ln T) for abruptly changing arms. A window of 0.2 of that keeps exploring and costs regret; the theory value is the minimum for Beta-SWTS.
numbers: K=10 arms, T=50,000, 50 runs, Bernoulli. Plain TS is best in the first stationary phase and degrades after changes; Beta-SWTS is best from the start of phase 2 (about t=12,000). Sensitivity grid: window exponents 0.2, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.8 of T.
limits: T=5e4 and 10 arms; nothing below a few hundred pulls. My arithmetic: sqrt(T ln T) at T=30 is about 10, a third of the run, so 'window' and 'no window' are nearly the same at our horizon.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: the literature shows windows helping only once stationary stretches are much longer than the window. No tested system uses one at a few dozen pulls. Keep plain TS, optionally with a stall reset.

source: Raj and Kalyani (2017) Taming Non-stationary Bandits: A Bayesian Approach (discounted Thompson sampling)
finding: Discounts the Beta parameters so old evidence fades. Tested in rested and restless settings, with an optimistic variant.
numbers: 1000 independent runs, default horizon T=5000; sinusoidal environments with period 1000; a switching environment with arm probabilities changing at t=50, 100, 150, 200 and a 250-step cycle.
limits: Shortest change interval is 50 steps inside horizons in the hundreds to thousands. No tests at T under 100. Discount choices are tuned per environment.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: every discounted or windowed TS study I opened runs 200 to 50,000 pulls. No published test exists at 20 to 60 pulls; see d17 for my simulation.

source: Agrawal and Goyal (2013) Thompson Sampling for Contextual Bandits with Linear Payoffs (ICML)
finding: First regret guarantee for contextual Thompson sampling: high-probability regret O~(d^{3/2} sqrt(T)), within a factor sqrt(d) of the lower bound.
numbers: Bound O~(d^{3/2} sqrt(T)) (or O~(d sqrt(T log N))). My arithmetic: this exceeds the trivial bound T whenever T < d^3, so for d=10 features it says nothing below T=1000.
limits: Theory only and worst case. The vacuity remark is my inference from the stated rate, not a claim in the paper. A state-keyed table with few states and shrinkage to a global mean is a simpler model than the one analysed.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: no theory supports a rich contextual bandit at 30 pulls. A state-keyed bandit would split 30 pulls over several states, leaving about 3 to 10 per state across 8 operators. It needs partial pooling across states or a hand-set prior (see d10 for a 4-state hand design).

source: Jamieson and Talwalkar (2016) Non-stochastic Best Arm Identification and Hyperparameter Optimization (AISTATS)
finding: Successive Halving for arms whose loss sequence converges as resource grows. Needs no knowledge of the gaps. Beats uniform allocation and, in their tests, UCB-type best-arm rules on hyperparameter search.
numbers: Table 1 compares budget needs: uniform allocation needs a multiple of the Successive Halving budget on hard instances. Their SVM experiments say Successive Halving finds good settings 'more than an order of magnitude' faster than uniform and than LUCB, lil'UCB and EXP3 baselines.
limits: Arms are training runs with converging losses, not i.i.d. judgments, and the advantage over UCB depends on that. Budgets are in thousands of resource units. Not an LLM study.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 background: halving wins when partial results predict final ones. For choosing among answers with about 5 checks each, evaluations are i.i.d. judgments, so the d18 simulation is the closer match.

source: Own simulation (Python, random module) of gap 1: 8 operators, 20, 40 and 60 pulls
finding: Bernoulli arms. 'Hard': best arm 0.35, others U(0.10,0.30). 'Easy': best 0.50, others U(0.10,0.30). 'Typical': all means Beta(2,5), best is the maximum. 3000 runs per cell. Regret is expected successes lost versus always pulling the best arm. TS with flat Beta(1,1) cuts regret versus uniform by 6 to 13 percent (hard) and 14 to 33 percent (typical); UCB1 (c=sqrt2) by 4 to 7 percent (hard) and 6 to 18 percent (typical). Epsilon-greedy 0.1 and UCB with c=0.5 often beat flat TS at these horizons.
limits: Synthetic and my own design; arm distributions and Bernoulli rewards are assumptions. Standard errors not computed (3000 runs); ignore differences under about 0.15. Flat priors make TS slow here: with 8 arms and 20 pulls it spends many pulls on untried arms. Not evidence about real operator logs, which is what gap 1 asked for.
agent_relevance: Gap 1, partly answered by simulation: at 8 arms and under 60 pulls, a fixed best guess that is right even 30 percent of the time beats every learner with a flat prior, and exploit-heavy rules (epsilon 0.1, UCB c=0.5) beat flat TS. A bandit pays off only with an informative start or more pulls. Needs confirming on real logs.

source: Own simulation of gap 5: informative priors, right and wrong, 8 operators, 30 pulls
finding: One arm gets a prior with mean 0.4 and strength st pseudo-counts, all others mean 0.2. In the 'right' case the flagged arm is the best arm; in the 'wrong' case it is a random other arm. 3000 runs, T=30.
numbers: Regret. Hard env (uniform 3.92, flat TS 3.65): st=2 right 3.39 / wrong 3.67; st=4 3.13 / 3.74; st=8 2.71 / 3.81; st=16 1.95 / 3.98. Typical env (uniform 7.47, flat TS 6.00): st=2 5.38 / 6.13; st=4 4.69 / 6.26; st=8 3.60 / 6.50; st=16 2.24 / 7.11. A 50/50 mix of right and wrong priors beats flat TS up to st=16 in both environments (hard 2.97 vs 3.65; typical 4.67 vs 6.00).
limits: The prior is concentrated on one arm, a strong form of error. Real prior errors would be a ranking. A wrong prior at st=16 in the typical env costs 1.1 over flat TS but is still below uniform (7.47). Synthetic.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a wrong prior of up to about 8 pseudo-counts costs 0.2 to 0.5 expected successes over 30 pulls here (1.1 at strength 16), while a right one saves 0.9 to 2.4 at strength 8. Use informative priors if they are right at least a third of the time, and cap strength near 4 to 8.

source: Own simulation of gap 8: capped counts vs plain TS, 8 operators, 30 and 60 pulls, with and without a mid-run switch
finding: Counts per arm are capped at C (successes rescaled) before sampling. Stationary and 'switch at T/2' environments, easy design (best 0.50, others 0.10 to 0.30). 3000 runs.
limits: No cap value changed regret by more than about 0.15 (noise). One switch only. Real operator values drift in other ways (they fall as parent quality rises).
agent_relevance: Gap 8: at 30 to 60 pulls a cap of 20 to 50 is inert, and caps of 5 to 10 bring no benefit even after a switch. Plain TS is enough at this horizon. Use a stall-triggered reset only if a stall rule is already in the scaffold.

source: Own simulation of gap 7: choosing the best of 10 or 30 candidates at about 5 evaluations each
finding: Candidates have Bernoulli success rates U(0.30,0.55) with one best at 0.55+gap. Methods: uniform allocation, Successive Halving, UCB1 (c=1 and c=0.5, pick best mean), TS (pick best posterior mean, or most pulled). 4000 runs per cell.
numbers: P(pick the true best) / simple regret. K=10, budget 50, gap 0.05: uniform 0.25/0.104; halving 0.28/0.095; UCB1 0.30/0.093; UCB c.5 0.32/0.089; TS 0.31/0.092. Gap 0.15: uniform 0.38; halving 0.47; UCB1 0.48; UCB c.5 0.54; TS 0.50. K=10, budget 100, gap 0.05: halving 0.40, UCB1 0.40, UCB c.5 0.43, TS 0.42, uniform 0.32. K=30, budget 150: gap 0.10 halving 0.28/0.115, UCB1 0.22/0.132, UCB c.5 0.28/0.117, TS 0.26/0.122, uniform 0.15; gap 0.20 halving 0.51, UCB1 0.41, UCB c.5 0.54, TS 0.52, uniform 0.26.
limits: Synthetic i.i.d. Bernoulli answers. Halving is the standard equal-budget-per-round version; UCB1 with c=1 over-explores when candidates outnumber the budget. Real candidates are correlated, which favours embedding-sharing methods (TRIPLE).
agent_relevance: Gap 7: every adaptive method beats uniform by 1.1x to 2x in P(best). Halving ties tuned UCB and TS within about 0.03 to 0.04, and beats plain UCB1 only when candidates are many (K=30). Not clearly better than bandit sampling at about 5 evaluations each. Halving is chosen for simplicity and no tuning.

source: Hong, Kveton, Zaheer, Ghavamzadeh (2022) Hierarchical Bayesian Bandits (AISTATS)
finding: Hierarchical Thompson sampling that learns a shared hyper-prior across many bandit tasks, with Bayes regret bounds that fall as the prior gets more informative.
numbers: Abstract and setting section: regret decreases with a more informative prior; the price of learning the hyper-parameter is low. Per-task horizon is a free parameter; I did not extract experiment tables.
limits: Only the abstract, introduction and setting were read. Theory assumes tasks are drawn i.i.d. from one distribution.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: if the agent runs many tasks, pool operator results across tasks into a hyper-prior (shrink toward the cross-task mean). That is the principled version of an informative prior from past tasks.
